title: Teamwork Contract
text: Milestone 1 asks your team to draft a teamwork contract. Below is a Quarto template to start from. It is based on a contract a past MDS team wrote for their DSCI 524 group project.

title: Teamwork Contract
text:
How to use the template

Create a file named team-contract.qmd. The contract is fairly personal, so it does not need to be in your public project repository.
Copy the template below (the button at the top right of the block copies it) and paste it into team-contract.qmd.
Replace everything in [square brackets]. The template is a starting point, not a form: change, add or remove anything so it describes how your team will work. Talk it through as a team before you write it down. A contract that is mostly the template with the brackets filled in will lose marks. See Milestone 1 for what a contract could cover.
Render it to PDF from the terminal:
quarto render team-contract.qmd
This creates team-contract.pdf next to it. The template uses Quarto’s built-in Typst format, so you do not need LaTeX installed.
Upload team-contract.pdf to Gradescope with your Milestone 1 submission.

title: Teamwork Contract
text:
Template
---
title: "Team contract"
subtitle: "DSCI 522, group [NUMBER]"
author:
  - "[TEAM MEMBER 1]"
  - "[TEAM MEMBER 2]"
  - "[TEAM MEMBER 3]"
  - "[TEAM MEMBER 4]" # delete this line for a team of three
date: today
format: typst
---

## Expectations

The time expected for group members to work on DSCI 522
will be a maximum of [NUMBER] hours a week,
unless all the team members agree to lengthen the time expected.
If team members cannot complete their sections within the maximum hours,
members should give notice on Slack at least 24 hours before the group submission deadline
to see if work should be redistributed or if the expected time should be increased.

All submissions are expected to meet the criteria of the milestones
as set out in the instructions.
This includes making sure all scripts are working,
creating tests for all our functions,
and using proper grammar in written submissions.

## Work distribution

At each weekly meeting, we will split the milestone into small tasks,
open a GitHub issue for each one, and assign it to a team member.
Over the course, everyone should do a similar amount of
coding, writing, and reviewing.
[DESCRIBE HOW YOUR TEAM WILL MAKE SURE THE WORK STAYS FAIR,
E.G., ROTATING WHO WRITES CODE VS. WHO WRITES THE REPORT.]

## Availability

Team members are not available at the following times:

- [TEAM MEMBER 1]: [E.G., EVENINGS AFTER 8 PM, SUNDAYS]
- [TEAM MEMBER 2]: [...]
- [TEAM MEMBER 3]: [...]
- [TEAM MEMBER 4]: [...]

We will not expect replies or reviews from someone during their unavailable times.

## Meetings

Meeting times were established during the initial team meeting held on [DATE].
Meetings will be held [PLACE, OR ONLINE ON ...] at the following times:

- [DAY]: [TIME]
- [DAY]: [TIME] (if needed)

The group will have a second formal meeting during the DSCI 522 lab on [DAY] at [TIME].
All members are expected to attend the meetings.
If a member cannot make a meeting,
written notice must be given 24 hours before the meeting to discuss alternative options.

## Communication

All project discussion outside of meetings will happen in GitHub issues:
ideas, suggestions, decisions, splitting up tasks, and meeting notes.
Work is submitted and reviewed through pull requests.
Slack is only for scheduling meetings and quick informal messages.
If an important decision is made on Slack, we will record it in a GitHub issue.

## Reviews

All members are expected to submit a pull request for their work
on the group project's repository on GitHub.com.
Members are expected to add teammates as reviewers,
so that every pull request is reviewed by another teammate.
Pull requests should be reviewed within [NUMBER] hours after creation.

## Use of AI

[DESCRIBE IF AND HOW YOUR TEAM WILL USE GENERATIVE AI (E.G., CHATGPT, CLAUDE, COPILOT),
AND FOR WHAT KINDS OF TASKS.]
Every team member is responsible for understanding and checking
any code or text they submit, whether or not AI helped write it.
Pull requests and GitHub issues are opened, reviewed, and merged by team members,
never by an AI agent or chat bot.
We will keep track of how we use AI so we can write the AI use statement in our README.

## Roles

There are two roles team members will be responsible for each week:

1. Scribe:
    - Responsible for taking notes at the meetings and in-class lab sessions,
      and adding them as a GitHub issue.
    - Responsible for sharing all notes and in-class activities with teammates.
2. Proof-reader:
    - Responsible for doing a final check of the submission before the deadline,
      to make sure all requirements are satisfied.

Roles will be rotated each week, so that each team member does each role at least once.

## Deadlines

Deadlines for individual items will be assigned during meetings.
The proof-reader will review the work on [DAY]
and ensure that the final version is ready for submission,
and will create the required GitHub release.

## Breach of contract

Failure to follow the team contract will result in a three-step warning system:

1. A written Slack notice that outlines the violation of the team contract
   and reminds the member of the team contract's conditions.
2. A meeting to discuss the behaviour,
   after which the member writes an agreement to follow the team contract.
3. Reaching out to the lab instructor or TAs about the issues with the teammate.

title: DSCI 522: Data Science Workflows
text:
Data-rich projects can quickly grow out-of-hand and become irreproducible in the absence of deliberate effort at organization, tool choice, and process. This course will teach basic principles of sound data scientific workflows and will develop skills implementing them in appropriate state-of-the-art systems and languages (e.g., Python and R).

title: DSCI 522: Data Science Workflows
text:
Learning Outcomes
By the end of the course, students are expected to be able to:

map a data analysis question to appropriate analysis
use a Git/GitHub to collaboratively work on a data analysis project
manage project software and environment dependencies using virtual environments and containers
write scripts and analysis pipelines for non-interactive data analysis
run literate coding documents non-interactively
automate data science workflows

title: DSCI 522: Data Science Workflows
text:
Deliverables
This is a project-based course. You will work in randomly assigned groups of three (or four, if needed) for the project milestones. There are also individual weekly assignments that act as stepping stones to the project milestones. Finally, because collaboration is so important in data science, we will be using a team work multiplier to adjust individual grades. A combination of peer evaluation and GitHub history will be used to evaluate this.






WarningLab attendance is mandatory



Students are expected to attend 100% of their scheduled lab hours and attendance will be taken at the beginning of each lab session. Students must make formal requests for academic concession in the event that they cannot attend a lab session by filling out this academic concession form and sending it to the course instructor. Applying for academic concession does not promise the granting of academic concession. Each application will be evaluated in the context of UBC’s Academic concession policy. Students missing more than 20% of the total scheduled lab hours for a course without having received an academic concession will receive a possible maximum course grade of 50% and an “F” standing for the course on the transcript. For all other policies, please see the general MDS policies.








NoteWeekly oral check-ins



Each week during lab, a member of the teaching team will have a short oral check-in (about 5 minutes) with you. Think of it as practice for a technical interview: we will ask you to walk us through part of your project, such as what a script does, how a test works, or why you made a particular design choice. These check-ins are not graded. They are a low-stakes chance to practice explaining your technical work out loud and to get feedback and help along the way.

title: DSCI 522: Data Science Workflows
text:
Policies

Academic Integrity
Academic integrity is a commitment to honesty, respect, responsibility, and accountability in academic work. It is foundational to teaching and learning and is a shared value of all members of the UBC community. In a project course, it also means being transparent with your teammates and the teaching team about how your work was produced.
Academic integrity in this course includes:

Submitting individual assignments that reflect your own understanding and intellectual contribution.
Contributing your fair share to your group’s project, and making sure your commits, pull requests, and reviews honestly represent the work you did.
Citing any code, text, or ideas you draw on from elsewhere (classmates outside your group, documentation, Stack Overflow, blog posts, generative AI tools, etc.), following the MDS program policy.
Respecting the licenses of any code, data, or other material you reuse in your project.
Following the generative AI policy below, including disclosing AI use for every deliverable.



Use of Generative AI
This course follows the MDS program’s Academic Integrity and Use of Generative AI policy. Assessment-specific instructions always take precedence over the general guidance below.
AI assistance is allowed. Generative AI tools (e.g., ChatGPT, Claude, GitHub Copilot, Cursor) are a real part of modern data science workflows, and you may use them in this course to brainstorm, explain concepts, debug errors, or help write code and documentation. That said, this course is about building your own skills in version control, environments, containers, testing, and pipelines. We strongly encourage you to attempt the work yourself first, and to use AI to support your learning rather than replace it. A useful question to ask yourself is: is this tool helping me understand the problem, or is it doing the thinking I am here to learn to do?
Disclose your AI use. For every milestone and individual assignment, you must state whether generative AI was used, including when it was not. If AI was used, please share:

which tool(s) and model(s) you used;
which parts of the work they were used for, and how; and
the instructions you gave the tool, such as any system prompt or agent configuration file (e.g., CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md, .cursor/rules/, .github/copilot-instructions.md), or, if you did not use one, a few representative example prompts.

For group milestones, please keep this disclosure in an AI_USAGE.md file in the root of your project repository and update it as the project evolves. For individual assignments, include the disclosure with your Gradescope submission. Disclosing AI use is not penalized, and it helps us give you useful feedback.
You remain responsible for everything you submit. Whether code was written by you, a teammate, or an AI tool, everyone in the group is responsible for its correctness, quality, and licensing. You should be able to explain what your code does, why it is designed that way, and how it fits into the rest of your project. Please do not merge code you have not read and understood.
A human opens every pull request. AI agents may help you write code, but a group member must review any generated changes and open, review, and merge pull requests themselves. Please do not let an AI agent push to your repository, open pull requests, or merge them on its own. Because GitHub history is used to evaluate teamwork, it should accurately reflect who did the work.
Communicate in your own words. When writing issues, pull request descriptions, code reviews, peer reviews, and team work reflections, please use your own words. AI may help with translation or grammar editing. Much of what you learn in this course comes from these conversations with your teammates.
Weekly check-ins. As described in Deliverables, the teaching team will have a short, ungraded oral check-in with each of you during lab every week, as practice for technical interviews. We may ask you to walk us through any part of your project, including code that was written with the help of AI. If someone is not yet able to explain work they contributed, we will follow up to better understand how the work was produced and to support their learning. Where needed, this may also include steps under UBC’s academic misconduct procedures.
Protect private information. Do not share confidential, private, or sensitive information with AI tools, including personal information about yourself, your teammates, or other students (for example, peer review content or team work reflections).
If you are unsure whether a particular use of AI is appropriate, please ask the teaching team before you submit your work.
Academic misconduct
Violations of academic integrity (i.e., academic misconduct) may lead to serious consequences. For more details, please see UBC’s Academic Integrity website, the Academic Calendar Statement on Academic Misconduct, and UBC’s guidance on Generative AI.
Parts of this AI policy are adapted from the earthaccess AI policy, which is based on the SciPy and SymPy AI policies.


General Program Policies

Please see the general and genAI use policies in MDS policies.
Please review General Lab Instructions
Check the MDS Rubrics for grading criteria.

title: Individual assignment 1
text:
This assignment will provide practice in the context of version control and will prepare you to collaborate on your group projects for this course. Follow the instructions listed below. You will be graded for completion.

Create a new public repository on GitHub.com named learning-about-version-control. Make sure the repository:

Includes a README.md that has a heading that says “Learning about Version Control” and has your name listed as the author.








Importantgithub.com not https://github.ubc.ca/



Make sure you do this in your own personal public GitHub account. Do not make this in the UBC github.



Clone your learning-about-version-control repository to your local computer.
Create and resolve a merge conflict 😱!

On GitHub.com, open your README.md, click the pencil (edit) icon, and add a line that says “Solving merge conflicts is easy!”. Commit the change on GitHub.
On your local computer (without pulling first!), add a line in the same place in the README, but this time write “Solving merge conflicts is soooooo hard!”
Add and commit your local changes to the README.md, then try to push. Git will reject the push, because GitHub has a commit you don’t have locally yet.
Pull the changes from GitHub with git pull --no-rebase. This is when the merge conflict appears. (The --no-rebase tells git to merge the two versions. Without it, newer versions of git stop and ask you how to combine them.)
Resolve the merge conflict on your local computer so that the line reads “Solving merge conflicts takes conscious effort, but I can do it!”. Take a screenshot while you are resolving the conflict (with the conflict markers <<<<<<<, =======, >>>>>>> visible) to show you did this.
Add and commit the resolved file, then push to your remote repository on GitHub.com.

Create and accept a pull request!

Create a new Git branch on your local version control repository named opinions and switch to that branch.
Edit your README.md so that you add at least one sentence about what you like most about version control, and add at least one sentence about what you find most challenging/confusing/frustrating about version control (we all have opinions on this one…). Add and commit your changes to local version control.
Push the changes to the README.md that you made on the opinions branch to the remote repository on GitHub.com.
Visit GitHub.com and create a pull request to suggest that the changes on the opinions branch should be merged into the main branch.
Merge the pull request you opened, so your changes from the opinions branch go into the main branch.

title: Individual assignment 1
text:
Submission Instructions
Follow the instructions for submission on Gradescope. Enter the URL and your explanation into Gradescope directly, and upload the screenshot there: there is no PDF to make. You will submit:

the URL of the GitHub.com repository you created and worked on for this assignment (it will be something like: https://github.com/<YOURUSERNAME>/learning-about-version-control). We will check its commit history and its Pull requests tab.
the screenshot of your resolved merge conflict
an explanation (2-3 sentences and in your own words) of why it is useful to work in a branch-pull-request workflow instead of working by directly committing each change to the main branch.
